clue.text: Queen heard brief word of thanks, touring a former British protectorate

indicators.note: touring means travelling round, so the queen-plus-thanks pair goes around the letter a
heard says the short thank-you is taken as it sounds, giving a word that sounds the same in non-rhotic speech

parts.note: ta is the informal British shortened word for thanks

explanation.surface: A queen, offered a curt thank-you, sets off on a tour of an old British protectorate in the Gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' turns TA into TAR, which sounds the same in southern British speech; 'touring' puts Q plus TAR around A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulf state was under British protection until it became independent in 1971.

clue.text: In America, change direction, fae ing south

parts.note: a quarter is one of the four compass directions or regions

explanation.surface: Changing course in the US to head south.
explanation.walkthrough: Quarters are US 25-cent coins, so loose change in America.
explanation.definitionFit: American loose change is made up largely of quarter-dollar coins.

clue.text: Chaotic situation, it's plain, gets out of control

indicators.note: getting out of control suggests disorder, so the letters of it's plain are rearranged

explanation.surface: An obvious statement that a situation is spiralling into chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailspin is literally an aircraft's spiralling dive, figuratively a state of chaotic panic.

clue.text: Clever chap in test cricket, so versatile

indicators.note: versatile means turning readily to different forms, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gifted all-rounder in test cricket is so adaptable.
explanation.walkthrough: Test cricket is the five-day international form of the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a rocket scientist is an idiom for someone very intelligent.

clue.text: Holidays by the sea for the guys

indicators.note: by means next to, so the holiday word sits beside the sea word

parts.note: the main is a poetic term for the open sea
stays are short visits or holidays

explanation.surface: Seaside breaks are what the lads go for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guys' looks like men, but it means the ropes that hold up a mast or tent.
explanation.definitionFit: Mainstays are the chief supporting ropes of a ship, as guys are supporting ropes.

clue.text: Regular participants in mean, ugly rugby scrum

indicators.note: regular means at even intervals, so alternate letters of mean, ugly are taken

explanation.surface: Nasty, ugly forwards in a rugby melee.
explanation.definitionFit: A maul is a loose rugby scrum formed round a player holding the ball.

clue.text: South of Bury, express highway

indicators.note: in a down clue, south of means below, so the express word follows

parts.note: to inter is to bury
to state is to express

explanation.surface: A fast road running south of the town of Bury.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town near Manchester, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An interstate is a US highway connecting states.

clue.text: To avoid casual employment, per haps, get on your bike?

definitions.text: To avoid casual employment, per haps, get on your bike?

parts.words: To avoid casual employment, per haps, get on your bike?
parts.note: cycling instead of walking means footwear such as casuals is not worn down; get on your bike also echoes a call to find a job

explanation.surface: Advice to find work rather than shun odd jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'casual employment' looks like temp work, but casuals are shoes, and employment means use; the clue was OCR'd as 'per haps' for 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to avoid walking, so riding a bike preserves your soles.

clue.text: A shallow lake in England and in Europe?

parts.note: a broad is one of the shallow lakes of the Norfolk Broads in eastern England

explanation.surface: A lake in England, and others on the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: For a British speaker, being in Europe is being overseas, in a foreign country.

clue.text: Man in the street on occasion falling short

indicators.note: falling short means not reaching the end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: an event is an occasion

explanation.surface: An ordinary bloke sometimes falls short.
explanation.walkthrough: EVENT loses its last letter T to give EVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Steven is a man's first name.

clue.text: Officer you said enters area surrounded in battle

indicators.note: enters means goes into, so the officer and the spoken word go inside the area-plus-surrounded run

parts.note: girt is an old word for surrounded or encircled
NCO is a non-commissioned officer

indicators.note: said tells us the word you is spoken, and the letter U sounds like it

parts.note: the word you, which the letter U sounds like

explanation.surface: An officer in a besieged area speaks to you about a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounded' looks like part of the battle picture but is the old past participle GIRT; 'enters' puts the officer and the spoken 'you' into it.
explanation.definitionFit: The battle of 1415 in northern France where Henry V's army defeated the French.

clue.text: For example churchman brought back emblem of office for bishop

indicators.note: brought back means returned, so the two pieces together are read in the reverse direction

parts.note: EG abbreviates the Latin exempli gratia, for example
Rev is short for Reverend, a churchman

explanation.surface: A clergyman returns a bishop's symbol of office, as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: EG + REV run backwards gives VERGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A verge is a rod or staff carried before a bishop or dignitary as a symbol of office.

clue.text: Elephant carrying us throughout awkward trek

indicators.note: carrying means holding inside, so the reworked trek holds the word us
awkward suggests something clumsily arranged, so the letters of trek are rearranged

explanation.surface: An elephant bears us through a difficult trek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' scrambles the trek; 'carrying' wraps the result round us, and 'throughout' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tusker is an elephant or boar with well-developed tusks.

clue.text: Sea carries sailors round port

indicators.note: carries means holds within, so the sea word contains the sailors

parts.note: the briny or brine is the sea

indicators.note: round means turned about, so the sailors word is read backwards

parts.note: ABs are able seamen, sailors

explanation.surface: The ocean bears sailors around to a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea' looks like the definition, but it is the container; 'round' turns the sailors and 'carries' puts them inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Brisbane is a major Australian port city on the Brisbane River.

clue.text: Hear man ring celebrities up in garden

parts.note: to get someone is to hear or understand them

indicators.note: ring means encircle, so the man word goes round the reversed celebrities

parts.note: he is a man, a male

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: names are famous people, big names

explanation.surface: Listen to a man phoning stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear man ring' suggests a telephone call; 'up' turns the celebrities, read upwards in this down clue, and 'ring' puts the man round them.
explanation.definitionFit: Gethsemane is the garden where Jesus prayed before his arrest.

clue.text: Check department admitting pressure in second Ofsted visit?

parts.note: to rein is to check or restrain

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the department word takes in the pressure letter

parts.note: a section is a department
P is the symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: An inspection discovers a department letting in pressure during a repeat visit.
explanation.walkthrough: Ofsted is the UK's schools inspectorate; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A second visit from inspectors is a repeat inspection, a re-examination of the school.

clue.text: Development of fine photograph

parts.note: F is the pencil-grading abbreviation for fine
to shoot is to photograph

explanation.surface: A developed photo of a fine subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Development' suggests film processing, but it is a growth.
explanation.definitionFit: An offshoot is a side growth, something developed from a main body.

clue.text: African resettled in English terrain

indicators.note: resettled means moved to new places, so the letters of terrain are rearranged

explanation.surface: An African moved to the English countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: An Eritrean is a native of Eritrea, in the Horn of Africa.

clue.text: Anti-abortionist fixed it for the girl

indicators.note: fixed means altered or rigged, so the words it for the girl are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone opposed to abortion rigged things for a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A campaigner holding that the unborn have a right to life opposes abortion.

clue.text: Still an irritation for the listener?

definitions.meaning: crackling interference heard on a radio

explanation.surface: A quiet moment, or an annoyance to a radio listener.
explanation.definitionFit: Static means motionless, and also atmospheric noise on radio reception.

clue.text: At home, managed to pick up article that's behind the wardrobe

indicators.note: in a down clue, pick up means lift, so the two pieces are read upwards

parts.note: in means at home
ran means managed
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Settled at home, someone manages to collect an item from behind a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: IN + RAN read upwards gives NARNI, then A.
explanation.definitionFit: In C. S. Lewis's books, the land of Narnia is reached through the back of a wardrobe.

clue.text: Model tracking system used to teach class?

definitions.meaning: a toy layout of locomotives running on rails
to instruct a group, read as two words: coach a set

explanation.surface: A model railway described as a teaching aid.
explanation.definitionFit: A toy railway with track and engines is sold as a set; to coach a group is literally the phrase.

clue.text: Dog given fish to eat, filleted

parts.note: bass is a fish

indicators.note: filleted means the insides are cut out, leaving only the first and last letters of eat

explanation.surface: A dog is given fish to eat, with the bones removed.
explanation.definitionFit: The basset is a short-legged hound breed.

clue.text: Behind rising, along with others

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read upwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: late means behind time

explanation.surface: Running late as the others get up.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin abbreviation means and others, used in lists of authors.

clue.text: Some art on display

indicators.note: some means a part of, so the answer is a run of letters within art on display

explanation.surface: Part of an art exhibition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tondi are circular paintings or reliefs, works of art that hang on show.

clue.text: Individual pursues yen, tucking into a British cut of beef

indicators.note: pursues means follows, so the individual word comes after the rest
tucking into means pushing inside, so the yen word goes between a and British

parts.note: a yen is an itch, a longing
one is an individual

explanation.surface: Someone with an urge is eating a British cut of beef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking into' points to the yen going inside a + British; 'pursues' puts the individual word last. The aitchbone joint is a traditional British beef cut.
explanation.definitionFit: The aitchbone is the rump bone of cattle, and the beef joint cut over it.

clue.text: What proficient map reader will do to locate Churchill's place?

definitions.text: What proficient map reader will do
definitions.meaning: someone good with maps will plot a route skilfully, read as two words
the Kent country house where Winston Churchill lived

explanation.surface: Good navigation leads you to Churchill's home.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartwell in Kent was Winston Churchill's family home for forty years.

clue.text: Give away fixed amount one no longer needed

indicators.note: something no longer needed is discarded, so the one letter is dropped from the allowance word

parts.note: a ration is a fixed allowance
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Hand over a fixed allowance that is now surplus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no longer needed' tells you to drop the I (one) from RATION.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat on someone is to betray or inform on them, to give them away.
